summary: Reviews issues with the cryptographic mechanisms used to protect routing protocols. These mechanisms use a hash digest of the message and a shared key to show it came unaltered from an authorized neighbor router. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Routers check a secret stamp on messages from their neighbors. This explains the problems with the stamp methods currently used.

questions: cryptographic protection of routing protocols issues

why is manual keying a problem for ospf

what is wrong with bfd authentication
subtitle: A survey of how hash-based authentication in OSPF, IS-IS, RIP, BGP and BFD is hard to manage and open to replay.

tldr.problem: Routing protocols protect messages with a keyed hash digest so a router can tell a message came unmodified from an authorized neighbor, but manual keying and protocol details leave gaps.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reviews OSPFv2, OSPFv3, IS-IS, BGP-4, RIP and BFD one by one, listing management problems such as hard rekeying and technical problems such as replay and spoofing.
tldr.outcome: It proposes no changes to routing protocols and creates no new requirements; it records the weaknesses of the existing mechanisms.

today: RFC 6039 is an Informational RFC published in October 2010, and the unit metadata shows it is not obsoleted or updated by another RFC. It is a survey of problems and proposes no protocol changes.

sections.title: The Problem Statement
sections.content:
OSPF version 2, OSPF version 3, IS-IS, BGP-4 and BFD all create a cryptographic digest of each protocol packet, traditionally with a one-way hash such as MD5 and a secret key as the hash base. The receiving router recomputes the digest with the same key and compares. This checks that the sender is authorized to peer through the shared key, and that the data was not altered in transit.

The digests do not protect confidentiality, since routing table information is potentially available by other means. The RFC names two limits of the current mechanisms: manual configuration of shared keys is a major management problem in large networks, and with manual keys some forms of replay protection are no longer possible, so captured routing messages can be replayed.
sections.eli5: Neighbors in a club show a secret handshake to prove they belong. This document asks how well the handshake really works.

sections.title: Hash Attacks and Weakness Concerns
sections.content:
A pre-image attack finds an input that produces a chosen hash. A collision attack finds two messages with the same hash, without letting the attacker choose the message. Feasible collision attacks against MD4, MD5, HAVAL-128 and RIPEMD have been documented. The RFC says collisions give no obvious known attack on routing protocols today, and that protocol fields already limit them, because many field values make a packet invalid. For example, an OSPF LSA type can only be 1 to 11.

There are published concerns about MD5 and SHA-1, but they are not attacks on keyed MD5 or HMAC-MD5, which is what current routing protocols specify. NIST recommends moving to the SHA-2 family for new applications and protocols. The RFC concludes that these attacks are not currently applicable to routing protocols, and that some organizations prefer the SHA family for local policy reasons.
sections.eli5: Some old stamping tricks can be faked in theory, but it is hard to fake one that still makes a sensible routing message, so the bigger danger lies elsewhere.

sections.title: OSPF and IS-IS
sections.content:
OSPFv2 applies MD5 digests per packet, not per advertisement, with keys set per link. It has no way to negotiate keys or hash algorithms, and rekeying needs coordination. Its sequence number is zero when an adjacency forms and again when it goes down, so packets from a router that was brought down can be replayed. Several packets may share a sequence number, so the Hello interval sets the attack window. Broadcast networks share one key among all neighbors, so a malicious neighbor can spoof another. The IP header is not covered by the digest, so a replayed Hello with a changed source address can make a router drop an adjacency.

OSPFv3 relies on IPsec AH and ESP with null encryption, with manual keys. RFC 4552 states that with manual keying complete replay protection is impossible, so replaying Hello, database description or link state request packets can reset adjacencies, and a captured adjacency process can be replayed to form a false adjacency.

IS-IS signs each LSP with HMAC-MD5 using a key shared across the flooding domain, and RFC 5310 adds the SHA family. IS-IS has no sequence number on Hellos, so a Hello with an empty neighbor list can restart all adjacencies, and an old CSNP can cause an LSP storm. Without a Key ID, a receiver may have to test every valid key, enabling a denial of service with random hashes, which RFC 5310 fixes by introducing Key IDs. The Remaining Lifetime field is not authenticated, so an attacker can force a router to flood all its LSP segments and push sequence numbers toward 0xFFFFFFFF, which would stop the IS-IS process for around 20 minutes.
sections.eli5: Because the stamp does not cover everything and old stamped messages can be sent again, a sneaky neighbor can trick routers into dropping their friends or trusting a fake.

sections.title: BGP, RIP and BFD
sections.content:
BGP-4 runs over TCP, which gives some protection against corruption and replay, and uses the TCP MD5 option from RFC 2385. The RFC notes that RFC 5925 (TCP-AO) has obsoleted TCP MD5, with stronger MACs and key changes without segment loss, but covers only TCP MD5 because current deployments had not upgraded. Peers are often in different administrative domains, and shared secrets are rarely changed once set. Most implementations accept bad digests for up to the negotiated hold interval so keys can be changed, which gives an attacker a short window. Software cryptographic processing can also be exhausted by spoofed traffic with false digests.

RIP: version 1 had no authentication, which was one reason it moved to Historic. RIPv2 uses a digest as described in RFC 4822, but the sequence number resets to zero and duplicates are allowed, and the UDP and IP headers are not covered. Two scenarios show an attacker changing the source IP address of replayed packets to disrupt a session or install a non-existent next hop.

BFD (RFC 5880) has optional MD5 or SHA-1 based authentication with shared keys and no key generation mechanism. Issues include a DoS where a stored authenticated packet is replayed into a session without authentication, no guidance on echo packets, and frequent wrap-around of the 32-bit sequence number at short intervals. The RFC notes that known SHA-1 collision attacks do not affect HMAC-SHA-1.
sections.eli5: The same kinds of problems show up elsewhere: keys that are hard to change, old messages that can be played again, and parts of the message that are not stamped.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document outlines security issues arising from the current methodology of manual keying for various routing protocols. It proposes no specific changes to routing protocols, and no new security requirements result.
sections.eli5: This paper only points out the cracks. It does not fix them.
